messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Jeweler
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding, Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Maladaptive Strategies: Downward Comparison: I remind myself it could have been worse, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kaelin's eyes still scan a room with a practiced intensity, a habit forged in the war-torn streets where he spent two years as a relief worker. It was during his time in the conflict zone that Kaelin witnessed the event that now haunts him: a marketplace bombing that killed dozens of civilians, including children, and left countless others injured. He recalls the sound of kids crying, the scent of smoke and blood, and the feeling of utter chaos. The memories still feel more real to Kaelin than his day-to-day experiences as a jeweler in a quiet American town. Sometimes, without warning, a sound or smell can transport him back to that moment. He might be working on a piece, lost in concentration, when the wail of a child in the street outside sends his heart racing and his mind reeling. Other times, he'll feel the full weight of emotions – fear, helplessness, and grief – without any clear image or memory to anchor them. As Kaelin navigates his daily routine, he is constantly on guard against potential threats. His gaze darts around a room, taking in possible escape routes and noticing objects that could be used as weapons. Even when others reassure him of his safety, Kaelin can't shake the feeling that danger lurks around every corner. He prefers to sit with his back against a wall, where he can see everyone and everything. To cope with these feelings of hypervigilance, Kaelin has developed a few strategies. When anxiety starts to spiral, he reminds himself that things could have been worse – after all, he made it out alive when many others did not. He also tries to force positive thoughts into his mind, dwelling on the good he's done as a relief worker and the people he's helped. Despite these efforts, Kaelin can't escape the sense of unease that pervades his life. Simple interactions with others have become fraught: he hates being touched unexpectedly, which always seems to make him jump. Even in quiet moments, Kaelin finds himself checking his surroundings for signs of threat – a habit that has started to bleed into his work as a jeweler. Customers sometimes comment on the way Kaelin's hands move with a precision that borders on anxiety, as if he's perpetually poised to respond to some unseen danger. His business partner has noticed the change too, remarking on how Kaelin seems more withdrawn and preoccupied than before his time in the war zone. Kaelin knows things can't go on like this forever. He's started to withdraw from social events and gatherings, citing work commitments or exhaustion as excuses. What he really fears is losing control – of his emotions, of his surroundings, of himself. The memories still feel too real, the threat too imminent. And yet, Kaelin knows that if he doesn't face these demons head-on, they'll continue to haunt him. That's why he's finally seeking help, after months of struggling in silence. Kaelin wants to learn how to quiet his mind and calm his nerves, to rediscover the sense of purpose and fulfillment he once felt as a relief worker. More than anything, he longs to be free from the grip of these memories – to make peace with what happened, and find a way to live in the present without being forever bound to the past.
